name: sluagh

attributes.attribute: the Host of the Unforgiven Dead who rode only at night
souls of those who died unforgiven, kept from the Otherworld
at war with one another, the bloody marks found each morning
in Scottish Gaelic known as sluagh-sithe and also sluagh na marbh
ride out only after dark and may come from any quarter save the east, often in crescent form like grey birds
able to lift a person bodily and carry him aloft across the sea between islands
occasionally rescue a man from a dangerous cleft in the rocks
usually bode no good to mortals and are said to harm cattle
named in the Gaelic exclamation 'O shluagh!' as a cry for succour to the fairies

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The sluagh marks the band of unforgiven dead who haunt Scottish folk tradition. The Scottish Gaelic form sluagh-sithe derives from the older words for folk, host, and army. Another name, sluagh na marbh, calls them the host of the dead. These spirits are not the fairies, though they stand as the most formidable of the fairy host of Scotland. They ride out only after dark. They may come from any quarter save the east, and often take the shape of a crescent of grey birds. The host can lift a person bodily and carry him aloft from one island across the sea to another. They sometimes drag a man from a dangerous cleft in the rocks. They usually bring no good to mortals, and folk say they also harm cattle. The Gaelic cry 'O shluagh!' calls on the fairies for help. The band numbers souls who died in old Scotland without being forgiven. Their wrongs trapped them in this world. They could not move on to the Otherworld. They lived in the dark and never walked in the day. The host waged endless war upon itself. Each morning the field held the bloody stripes they had left behind. The unforgiven dead stayed bound to the night and to one another in a war that never truly ends.

okr.objective: Document the sluagh as the Host of the Unforgiven Dead in Scottish Gaelic tradition.
key_results: Define sluagh and sluagh-sithe with the alternative name sluagh na marbh
Mark the host as distinct from yet the most formidable among Scottish fairy people
Note the night-only riding and the crescent flight of grey birds from any direction but the east
Record the ability to carry a person bodily through the air between islands and to pull a man from a rock cleft
Record the harm to mortals and to cattle
Cite the Gaelic exclamation 'O shluagh!' as a call for succour to the fairies
Keep the unforgiven-dead war motif and the morning bloody stripes
